Chapter 11

Fitting It All Together

融会贯通

If you’ve made it this far, you already know: chaos doesn’t give out medals for endurance. But you’re still here, and that matters. Perhaps you’re reading this at your desk between incidents, on your phone during an excruciating planning meeting, or at home after another day of trying to bring order to chaos. Wherever you are, take a moment to acknowledge that you’re still here, still fighting, still trying to get better at this impossible job.

如果你读到了这里，你已经知道：混乱并不会因为你“扛得住”就给你发奖章。但你依然还在，而这一点很重要。也许你正在工位上、在两起事故的间隙读这段；也许你正在一场折磨人的计划会上、用手机偷读；又也许你刚又熬了一天、试图给混乱带来秩序，此刻正在家里读。无论你身在何处，花一点时间承认：你还在这里，还在战斗，还在努力把这份“不可能的工作”做得更好。

That persistence matters more than you might think. Because engineering leadership in chaos isn’t about having all the answers or following a perfect playbook. It’s about showing up, day after day, and making things a little bit better than they were yesterday. It’s about building momentum when everything wants to grind to a halt. It’s about creating clarity when fog is the natural state. And most importantly, it’s about helping your team thrive despite conditions that would make most people throw their hands up and walk away.

这种坚持，比你以为的更重要。因为混乱中的工程领导力，不在于拥有所有答案，也不在于照本宣科地遵循一本完美的剧本。它在于日复一日地出现，把事情做得比昨天好一点点。它在于当一切都想停摆时，去积累动能。它在于当迷雾才是常态时，去创造清晰。而最重要的是：在于帮助你的团队——在那些会让大多数人甩手走人、放弃一切的条件下——依然茁壮成长。

We’d also be remiss not to remind you that sometimes, walking away is the right choice. Persistence is powerful, but not at the expense of your mental and physical health. Sometimes situations can’t be improved or fixed. If you feel burnt out or that you’re treading water without making forward progress, think carefully about what the best outcome is for you. Taking care of yourself first is always the right choice.

我们也必须提醒你：有时候，转身离开才是正确的选择。坚持很有力量，但不能以牺牲你的身心健康为代价。有些局面就是无法改善、无法修复。如果你感到倦怠，或觉得自己一直在原地扑腾、毫无前进，那就认真想想：对你而言最好的结局是什么。先照顾好自己，永远是正确的选择。

Throughout this book, we’ve thrown a lot at you: technical principles, user stories, budget spreadsheets, vendor management, requests for comments (RFCs), retrospectives, metrics that matter, and metrics that can mislead. Each chapter has its own universe of chaos and disorder, along with approaches, tools, and techniques to deal with that. Now it’s time to step back and see how it all connects, because the real power isn’t in excelling in any single aspect of engineering leadership; it’s in understanding how these pieces work together to create something greater than the sum of their parts.

整本书里，我们一股脑儿塞给了你太多东西：技术原则、用户故事、预算表格、供应商管理、意见征询（RFC）、回顾会、真正重要的指标、以及会误导人的指标。每一章都有自己那一重混乱与失序的宇宙，也配有应对它们的方法、工具和技巧。现在是时候退一步，看看这一切如何相互连接了——因为真正的力量，不在于把工程领导力的某一个方面做到极致；而在于理解这些碎片如何协同工作，创造出一个大于各部分之和的东西。

The Symphony of Chaos

混乱的交响

As you’ve discovered in this book, we both love a metaphor. So here’s (almost) your final one: the reality of engineering leadership.

正如你在本书中已经发现的，我们俩都热爱打比方。那么（几乎）这是最后一个比方了：工程领导的现实。

As the engineering leader, you’re the conductor of the symphony—the maestro—and it’s up to you to guide your team—strings, brass, woodwinds, percussion—through the chaos with the cues you give from your podium and the feedback you receive from your orchestra as they perform. You stand at the center of a complex system, each part demanding your attention. Your people form the foundation, the core strength of everything you build. Your technical infrastructure is essential and enabling, yet requiring constant vigilance. Your processes flow beneath the surface, often invisible but critical to keeping work moving forward. Your metrics provide the necessary feedback, confirming whether what you’re building can withstand pressure. And you’re there in the middle of it all, armed with incomplete information and an evolving plan, working to align everyone toward the same goal while priorities shift, requirements change, and unexpected crises demand immediate response.

作为工程领导者，你是这场交响乐的指挥——是 maestro——你要靠自己在指挥台上给出的手势、以及乐团演奏时反馈给你的声音，引导你的团队——弦乐、铜管、木管、打击乐——穿过混乱。你站在一个复杂系统的中心，每个部分都在索要你的注意力。你的人构成了地基，是你所建一切的核心力量。你的技术基础设施必不可少、赋予团队能力，却需要时刻保持警惕。你的流程在水面之下流淌，常常不可见，却对让工作继续前进至关重要。你的指标提供必要的反馈，确认你正在建造的东西能否承受压力。而你就站在这一切的中央，手里握着不完整的信息和一份不断演变的计划，努力让所有人朝同一个目标对齐——与此同时，优先级在变、需求在变、意料之外的危机要求你立刻响应。

In calm conditions, you could focus methodically on each element. You’d have time to be deliberate, to refine your approach, and to build systematically toward excellence. In the reality of constant change, you’re managing shifting timelines, team transitions, and strategies that evolve weekly, all while navigating urgent demands from every direction. Success isn’t about creating the perfect system under ideal circumstances; it’s about maintaining forward momentum and delivering value despite the turbulence.

在风平浪静时，你可以有条不紊地逐个打磨每个要素。你会有时间从容不迫、优化方法、系统性地朝卓越建造。但在持续变化的现实里，你要同时管理不断移动的时间线、团队的交接、以及每周都在演变的战略，还要应对从四面八方涌来的紧急需求。成功，不在于在理想条件下造出完美的系统；而在于即便在颠簸中，仍能保持前进的动能、持续交付价值。

This is why everything we’ve discussed in this book interconnects so deeply. Your technical principles aren’t just about the quality of your code; they shape how your team collaborates and makes decisions. Communication isn’t just about sharing information; it builds the psychological safety that enables innovation. And your metrics aren’t just numbers on a dashboard; they are the feedback loops that tell you whether your other efforts are working. Every aspect of engineering leadership influences every other aspect, creating either virtuous cycles that build momentum or vicious cycles that compound dysfunction.

这就是为什么本书讨论的一切都如此深刻地相互关联。你的技术原则不只关乎代码质量；它们塑造团队如何协作、如何做决策。沟通不只关乎分享信息；它构建起让创新得以发生的心理安全。而你的指标不只是仪表盘上的数字；它们是反馈回路，告诉你其他种种努力是否奏效。工程领导力的每一个方面都在影响其他每一个方面，要么制造出积累动能的良性循环，要么制造出放大功能失调的恶性循环。

The Foundation: People and Safety

地基：人与安全感

Let’s start with the most important aspect: people. We’ve said it before, but it bears repeating because it’s so easy to forget when you’re drowning in technical debt and deadlines: without psychological safety, nothing else works. If there is no trust, there is no team. Instead, it’s just a group of people cashing checks and keeping their heads down. It’s not your beautiful technical architecture, your elegant processes, or your comprehensive metrics—it’s nothing.

我们从最重要的方面开始：人。我们之前说过，但值得再说一遍——因为当你被技术债和截止日期淹没时，太容易忘记：没有心理安全，其他一切都不奏效。没有信任，就没有团队。有的只是一群人，领着工资、低着头混日子。再美的技术架构、再优雅的流程、再周全的指标——全都毫无意义。

— 原书第 248 页 —

When your team doesn’t feel safe to speak up, admit mistakes, challenge ideas, or show vulnerability, you’re operating at a massive disadvantage. You might not see it immediately. People are good at hiding their fears, going through the motions, and delivering just enough to avoid attention. However, over time, the absence of psychological safety creates a kind of organizational scar tissue that makes everything more difficult. Innovation slows down because people are unwilling to take risks. Problems fester because no one wants to be the messenger. Technical debt accumulates because admitting its existence feels like admitting failure.

当你的团队不敢发声、不敢认错、不敢质疑想法、不敢展现脆弱时，你正在巨大的劣势下运作。你可能一时看不见。人们很擅长隐藏恐惧、走过场、只做到刚好不被注意到的程度。然而，久而久之，心理安全的缺失会形成一种组织疤痕组织，让一切都变得更难。创新慢下来，因为人们不愿冒险。问题溃烂，因为没人愿意当那个报信的人。技术债不断累积，因为承认它的存在就像承认失败。

Building psychological safety in chaotic environments is particularly challenging because chaos itself often feels unsafe. When priorities shift daily, when leadership changes frequently, or when the company’s future feels uncertain, people naturally become defensive. People protect themselves by keeping their heads down, avoiding anything that might make them a target, and doing precisely what they’re told—and nothing more.

在混乱环境里建立心理安全尤其困难，因为混乱本身就让人感到不安全。当优先级天天变、领导层频繁更迭、或公司的未来显得捉摸不定时，人们自然会进入防御状态。人们通过低头自保、回避任何可能让自己成为靶子的事、以及只严格做被吩咐的事（绝不多做一点），来保护自己。

This is where your role as a leader becomes crucial. You become the stability, not by pretending the chaos doesn’t exist or by promising you can stop it, but by being consistent in how you show up, how you respond to problems, and how you treat people. When someone raises a concern, you listen. When someone makes a mistake, you focus on learning. When someone challenges your ideas, you thank them for their candor. These small acts, repeated consistently over time, create pockets of safety that gradually expand until they encompass the entire team.

这正是你作为领导者的角色变得关键的地方。你成为那个稳定器——不是靠假装混乱不存在，也不是靠许诺你能阻止它，而是靠在“如何出现、如何回应问题、如何待人”上保持一致。当有人提出担忧时，你倾听。当有人犯错时，你聚焦于学习。当有人质疑你的想法时，你感谢他们的坦诚。这些微小的举动，随时间一致地重复，会造出一个个安全的小角落，逐渐扩大，直到覆盖整个团队。

But safety alone isn’t enough. You also need capability and cohesion. A safe team that can’t execute is just a support group. This environment is where all those processes and practices we’ve discussed come into play. They become the scaffolding that enables teams to work together effectively. User stories create shared understanding. Code reviews spread knowledge. RFCs encourage thoughtful design. Retrospectives promote continuous improvement. Each practice, when implemented thoughtfully and maintained consistently, adds another layer of capability to your team.

但光有安全感还不够。你还需要能力和凝聚力。一个安全却不能执行的团队，只是一个互助小组。在这种环境下，我们讨论过的所有流程和实践才真正派上用场。它们成为脚手架，让团队能够有效协作。用户故事创造共同理解。代码评审传播知识。RFC 鼓励深思熟虑的设计。回顾会推动持续改进。每一项实践，只要经过深思熟虑地落地、并被一致地坚持，就会为你的团队再添一层能力。

The Lighthouse: Direction, Not Drift

灯塔：方向，而非随波逐流

Once you have a foundation of safety and capability, you need direction. This might seem paradoxical in chaos, where the future is inherently unpredictable. How can you set a direction when you don’t know what next month will bring, let alone what next year will bring? The answer is that direction in chaos isn’t about predicting the future; it’s about creating coherence in the present.

一旦你有了安全感和能力的地基，你就需要方向。这在混乱中似乎有点悖论——未来本就不可预测。你连下个月会带来什么都不知道，更别说明年，又怎么设定方向？答案是：混乱中的方向，不在于预测未来；而在于在当下创造一致性。

Think of direction like this: you’re not plotting a course to a specific destination, you’re choosing which general direction to head. North might be “improve reliability.” Northeast might be “reduce technical debt while expanding into new markets.” East might be “rapid feature development.” You might not know exactly where you’ll end

可以这样理解方向：你不是在画一条通往某个具体目的地的航线，你是在选择大致朝哪个方向走。正北可能是“提升可靠性”。东北可能是“在拓展新市场的同时减少技术债”。正东可能是“快速开发功能”。你也许不知道最终会抵达

— 原书第 249 页 —

up, but you know which way you’re moving—and, more importantly, which ways you’re not moving.

哪里，但你知道自己在往哪个方向走——更重要的是，你知道自己不在往哪些方向走。

This is where those technical principles we discussed become so powerful. They’re not rigid rules to constrain your team; they’re guideposts that help your team make consistent decisions even when specific requirements are unclear. When an engineer faces a choice between a simple solution and a complex one, “simplicity first” provides direction. When a team debates whether to document a decision, “documentation as communication” settles the question. These principles create alignment without requiring constant coordination, which is essential when you don’t have time (or the desire) for endless meetings and debates.

这正是我们讨论过的那些技术原则变得如此有力量的地方。它们不是束缚团队的僵硬规则；它们是路标，帮你的团队在具体需求尚不清晰时，也能做出一致的决策。当一名工程师在简单方案和复杂方案之间做选择时，“简单优先”提供了方向。当一个团队在争论是否要把某个决策写下来时，“文档即沟通”了结了争论。这些原则无需持续协调就创造了对齐——而当你没有时间（也没有意愿）开没完没了的会、争论个不停时，这一点至关重要。

Setting direction also means making peace with incompleteness. In chaos, you’ll never have all the information you want, you’ll never be certain that you’re making the right choice, and you’ll never be able to predict all the consequences of your decisions. But as we’ve emphasized throughout this book, action beats inaction almost every time. A decent decision made today is usually better than a perfect decision made next month. Because in chaos, next month’s context will be completely different anyway.

设定方向，也意味着与“不完整”和解。在混乱中，你永远不会拥有想要的全部信息，永远不会确定自己做的是正确选择，也永远无法预测决策的全部后果。但正如我们在本书中反复强调的：行动几乎永远胜过不行动。今天做出的一个过得去的决策，通常好于下个月才做出的一个完美决策。因为在混乱中，下个月的情境反正会完全不同。

This means being thoughtfully decisive by gathering sufficient information to make a mostly reasonable choice, communicating that choice, and then committing to it long enough to see results. It means being willing to adjust when new information emerges, but not second guessing yourself every time someone raises a concern. It’s a delicate balance, and you won’t always get it right. But the teams that thrive in chaos are those whose leaders can make decisions and stick with them long enough for the team to build momentum.

这意味着：深思熟虑地果断决策——收集足够信息以做出一个大体合理的选择，把这个选择沟通出去，然后坚持足够长的时间以看到结果。它意味着当新信息出现时愿意调整，但也不是每次有人提出担忧就反复自我怀疑。这是一种微妙的平衡，你不会每次都做对。但在混乱中茁壮成长的团队，其领导者都能做出决策、并坚持足够久，让团队得以积累动能。

The Engine: Process and Execution

引擎：流程与执行

With safety, capability, and direction in place, you need an engine that turns potential into reality. This is where process comes in. But this isn’t process as most people understand it—not a heavy, rigid, bureaucratic process that slows everything down. Instead, we’re talking about a lightweight, adaptable process that enables execution rather than constraining it.

有了安全感、能力和方向，你还需要一台把潜能转化为现实的引擎。这就是流程的用武之地。但这不是大多数人理解的那种流程——不是那种笨重、僵硬、官僚、把一切都拖慢的流程。相反，我们说的是一种轻量、可调整、赋能执行而非束缚执行的流程。

The key insight about process in chaos is that it should be just enough to prevent disorder, but not so much that it prevents adaptation. Think of it like the minimal amount of structure needed to keep things from falling apart: a daily standup that actually stays under 15 minutes and helps people coordinate, a simple Kanban board that makes work visible without requiring hours of grooming, or code review that catches problems without becoming a bottleneck. Each process should earn its keep by clearly making things better, and the moment it stops adding value, it should be simplified or eliminated.

关于混乱中流程的关键洞见是：它应当刚好足以防止失序，但又不能多到妨碍适应。把它想成“让事情不至于散架所需的最低限度结构”:一次真的能控制在 15 分钟以内、确实帮大家协调的每日站会；一块简单的看板，让工作可见却又不需要花几小时梳理；或者一种能抓住问题、却不会变成瓶颈的代码评审。每一项流程都必须靠“明确地让事情变好”来挣得自己的存在；一旦它不再增加价值，就该被简化或废除。

— 原书第 250 页 —

This is why, throughout the book, we’ve emphasized starting small and building up. It’s tempting, especially if you’re coming from a more structured environment, to try to implement all the processes you’re familiar with—sprint planning, backlog grooming, story pointing, retrospectives, demos, architecture reviews, and on and on. But in chaos, every process has a cost in terms of time, energy, and cognitive load. Your team only has so much capacity for process, and if you use it all up on ceremonies and meetings, there’s nothing left for actually building things.

这就是为什么全书我们都强调“从小处起步、逐步建立”。尤其是如果你来自一个更结构化的环境，你会很想把自己熟悉的所有流程都搬过来——冲刺计划、待办梳理、故事点估算、回顾会、演示、架构评审，等等。但在混乱中，每一项流程都有代价：时间、精力和认知负荷。你的团队能用于流程的产能就那么多；如果你把它全花在仪式和会议上，就没有剩下什么来真正建造东西了。

The art is in finding the minimal viable process for your current situation, and then evolving it as conditions change. When you’re in pure survival mode, all you need is a daily check-in and a shared list of priorities. As things stabilize, you should add lightweight planning sessions. As the team grows, you need more structured communication patterns. The process should grow organically in response to actual problems, not in anticipation of theoretical ones.

这门艺术在于：找到适合你当前处境的最小可行流程，然后随环境变化让它演进。当你处在纯粹的求生模式时，你只需要一次每日对齐和一份共享的优先级清单。当局势稳定下来，你应当加上轻量的计划会。当团队成长，你需要更结构化的沟通模式。流程应当回应真实问题而有机生长，而不是为预期中的理论问题提前搭建。

Execution in chaos also requires a different mindset about what constitutes success. In stable environments, you can aim for perfection, or at least something close to it. You can take the time to get things exactly right—to polish every edge, to optimize every algorithm. In chaos, perfection is the enemy of progress. You need to embrace “good enough” as a legitimate target, at least initially. In chaos, polished work is often irrelevant work. Ship the feature that solves 80% of the problem, and then iterate. Build the system that handles the common cases, and then add edge case handling as needed. Write the documentation that helps people get started, and then expand it based on actual questions.

混乱中的执行，还要求你对“什么算成功”抱持不同的心态。在稳定环境里，你可以追求完美，或至少接近完美。你可以花时间把事情做到完全正确——打磨每一个边角、优化每一个算法。但在混乱中，完美是进步的敌人。你需要把“足够好”接受为一个正当的目标——至少一开始如此。在混乱中，打磨得精美的工作常常是无关紧要的工作。发布那个解决了 80% 问题的功能，然后再迭代。搭建那个能处理常见情形的系统，然后按需补充边界情况处理。写下那份帮人入门的文档，然后基于真实问题再扩充它。

It’s not about lowering standards; it’s about recognizing that in chaos, momentum matters more than perfection. A team that ships something imperfect but useful every week will outperform a team that spends months crafting the perfect solution. Because by the time that ideal solution is ready, the problem it was supposed to solve has probably changed. The key is to be intentional about what you’re trading off and to have a plan for addressing those trade-offs over time.

这不是在降低标准；而是认识到：在混乱中，动能比完美更重要。一个每周都发布“不完美但有用”的东西的团队，会胜过一个花数月雕琢完美方案的团队。因为当那个理想方案终于就绪时，它原本要解决的问题可能已经变了。关键是：有意识地想清楚你在权衡什么，并计划好随时间如何处理这些权衡。

The Compass: Metrics and Measurement

罗盘：指标与度量

As your engine runs, you need a way to know if you’re actually making progress. This is where metrics come in—but again, not in the traditional sense. Not vanity metrics that make you look good in presentations. Not weaponized metrics used to punish teams that don’t meet arbitrary targets. Instead, we’re talking about metrics as a compass, helping you understand where you are and whether you’re moving in the right direction.

当你的引擎运转起来时，你需要一种办法来知道自己是否真的在前进。这就是指标的用武之地——但同样，不是传统意义上的那种。不是让你在汇报里好看的虚荣指标。不是用来惩罚那些没达到武断目标的团队的武器化指标。相反，我们说的是把指标当作罗盘：帮你理解自己身在何处、是否在朝正确的方向移动。

— 原书第 251 页 —

The biggest mistake is trying to measure everything, with dozens of metrics and endless dashboards. In chaos, you don’t have time to analyze all that data, and most of it isn’t actionable anyway. You end up with information overload that obscures rather than illuminates what’s really happening.

最大的错误，是试图度量一切：搞几十项指标、做无数个仪表盘。在混乱中，你没有时间分析所有那些数据，而且其中大多数本来也不可行动。最后你得到的是信息过载——它遮蔽、而不是照亮了正在发生的事。

Instead, focus on a small number of metrics that directly relate to your current challenges. If reliability is your biggest problem, track mean time to recovery and change failure rate. If delivery is the issue, measure cycle time and deployment frequency. If quality is suffering, monitor bug rates and test coverage. The key is to be selective and purposeful, and to choose metrics that will actually influence decisions rather than just creating pretty charts.

相反，要聚焦于少数几项与你当前挑战直接相关的指标。如果可靠性是你最大的问题，就追踪平均恢复时间和变更失败率。如果交付是问题，就度量周期时间和部署频率。如果质量在下滑，就监控 bug 率和测试覆盖率。关键是要有选择、有目的，选那些真正会影响决策的指标，而不只是为了做出漂亮的图表。

Remember, too, that metrics in chaos need to be treated differently from those in stability. In stable environments, you can set targets and expect steady progress toward them. However, in chaos, metrics will be messy, with wild swings that may have nothing to do with your team’s performance. A deployment might fail because a vendor had an outage. Cycle time might spike because half the team got pulled into an emergency. Bug rates might jump because you finally started tracking them properly.

也请记住：混乱中的指标，需要和稳定环境中的指标区别对待。在稳定环境里，你可以设定目标、并期待朝它稳步前进。但在混乱中，指标会很杂乱，会剧烈波动——而这些波动可能与你团队的表现毫无关系。一次部署失败，可能是因为某个供应商宕机了。周期时间飙升，可能是因为一半人被拉去处理紧急事故了。bug 率跳升，可能只是因为你终于开始正确地追踪它们了。

This is why context matters so much with metrics. Raw numbers without explanation are useless, and they’re actively misleading. Every metric should have a story that explains what it means, why it might be changing, and what (if anything) should be done about it. This requires more work than just making dashboards, but it’s essential for maintaining trust and making good decisions. Metrics without context are just numbers cosplaying as truth.

这就是为什么对指标来说，背景如此重要。没有解释的裸数字毫无用处，而且会主动误导人。每一项指标都应当有一个故事，解释它意味着什么、为什么可能在变、以及（如果需要）该对此做什么。这比做仪表盘要费更多功夫，但它对维持信任和做出好决策至关重要。没有背景的指标，只是在 cosplay 成真相的数字而已。

The Ecosystem: Building Beyond Your Team

生态：在团队之外建造

Your team doesn’t exist in isolation, especially during times of chaos. You and your team are part of a larger organism that includes other engineering teams, product, design, sales, support, leadership, and customers. Success requires navigating effectively, building bridges where they’re needed, and sometimes creating boundaries where they’re not.

你的团队并非孤立存在——尤其在混乱时期。你和你的团队是一个更大有机体的一部分，这个有机体包括其他工程团队、产品、设计、销售、支持、领导层和客户。成功需要你有效地穿行其间：在需要的地方架桥，有时在不需要的地方划界。

This is where all that work on communication and collaboration pays off. The RFC process isn’t just about making better technical decisions; it’s about creating visibility into those decisions for other teams. The documentation you write isn’t just for your future self; it’s for the support engineer trying to help a customer at 2:00 a.m. The metrics you track aren’t just for your team’s improvement; they’re for building confidence within leadership that the engineering team is delivering value despite the chaos.

这正是所有那些沟通与协作的功夫开始回报的地方。RFC 流程不只是为了做出更好的技术决策；它是为了让其他团队看见这些决策。你写下的文档不只是给未来的自己看的；它是给那位凌晨两点正在帮客户解决问题的支持工程师看的。你追踪的指标不只是为了团队自身的改进；它们是为了让领导层相信：尽管一片混乱，工程团队仍在交付价值。

Effective management in general becomes particularly crucial in chaotic environments. Your leadership teams are probably feeling the pressure too, dealing with their

一般意义上的有效管理，在混乱环境中变得格外关键。你的领导团队大概也在承受压力，正在应对他们

— 原书第 252 页 —

own chaos at the organizational level. So, they need confidence that engineering is under control, that problems are being addressed, and that progress is being made. This doesn’t mean hiding problems or pretending everything is fine. Rather, you need to be proactively communicating what’s happening, what you’re doing about it, and what you need from organizational leadership.

自己在组织层面的混乱。因此，他们需要信心：工程一切尽在掌控、问题正在被处理、进展正在取得。这不是要你隐藏问题、或假装一切都好。相反，你需要主动沟通：正在发生什么、你在做什么、你需要组织领导层提供什么。

The vendor and budget management aspects we discussed aren’t just about controlling costs; they’re about building an extended capability network. In chaos, you can’t build everything yourself. You need partners who can provide specialized capabilities, handle noncore functions, and scale with your needs. But these relationships require active management. Vendors need to understand your constraints and priorities. Contracts need to be flexible enough to adapt to changing conditions. Costs need to be predictable enough to plan around, even when everything else is unpredictable.

我们讨论过的供应商与预算管理，不只是为了控制成本；它们是为了建立一个扩展的能力网络。在混乱中，你不可能什么都自己造。你需要合作伙伴来提供专业能力、承接非核心职能、并随你的需求扩展。但这些关系需要主动经营。供应商需要理解你的约束和优先级。合同需要足够灵活，以适应不断变化的条件。成本需要足够可预测，以便围绕它做计划——即便其他一切都不可预测。

Cross-functional collaboration becomes even more critical in chaos because misalignment is incredibly expensive. When engineering teams build the wrong thing because requirements were unclear, when the product team promises features that can’t be delivered, or when sales teams set expectations that can’t be met, the resulting friction can bring everything to a halt. This is why investing in collaborative practices, shared language, and mutual understanding pays such high dividends. Every hour spent aligning with the product team saves days of rework. Every conversation with sales teams prevents a crisis with a customer. Every sync with the support team reveals problems that you didn’t know existed.

跨职能协作在混乱中变得更加关键，因为错位的代价极其高昂。当工程团队因为需求不清而做错了东西、当产品团队许诺了无法交付的功能、当销售团队设定了无法兑现的期望时，由此产生的摩擦能让一切停摆。这就是为什么在协作实践、共同语言和相互理解上的投资会带来如此高的回报。和产品团队对齐所花的每一小时，都省下了好几天的返工。和销售团队的每一次对话，都避免了一场与客户的危机。和支持团队的每一次同步，都揭示出一些你原本不知道存在的问题。

The Evolution: From Chaos to Capability

演进：从混乱到能力

Here’s something we haven’t talked about explicitly but that underlies everything in this book: chaos doesn’t last forever. Organizations either evolve beyond chaos, find stability and scale, or they fail. Your job as an engineering leader isn’t just to survive the chaos; it’s to help your organization evolve through it.

有一件事我们没有明说，但它是本书一切内容的底层逻辑：混乱不会永远持续。组织要么演进、走出混乱，找到稳定与规模；要么失败。你作为工程领导者的工作，不只是在混乱中活下来；而是帮助你的组织穿越混乱、实现演进。

This evolution doesn’t happen overnight, and it doesn’t happen linearly. You’ll have periods of progress followed by setbacks. You’ll solve one source of chaos only to discover another. You’ll build capabilities that become obsolete as the organization changes. This is normal and expected. You just need to focus on maintaining forward momentum, even when it feels like you’re taking two steps forward and one step back.

这种演进不会一夜发生，也不会线性发生。你会经历一段进展，接着遭遇挫折。你解决了一个混乱之源，结果又发现另一个。你建立的能力，会随着组织变化而过时。这很正常，也在预料之中。你只需要专注于保持前进的动能——即便感觉上是进两步、退一步。

Each of the practices and approaches we’ve discussed in this book builds organizational capability that persists beyond the immediate chaos. The psychological safety you create becomes part of the culture. The technical principles that you establish will guide future decisions. The processes that you implement will evolve. The metrics that you establish will create feedback loops that drive continuous improvement.

本书讨论的每一项实践和方法，都在构建一种超越眼前混乱而长期存在的组织能力。你创造的心理安全，会成为文化的一部分。你确立的技术原则，将指引未来的决策。你落地的流程，会不断演进。你建立的指标，会创造出驱动持续改进的反馈回路。

— 原书第 253 页 —

Layer by layer, you’re building an organization that can handle not only the current chaos but also future challenges.

一层一层地，你正在建造一个不仅能应对当前混乱、也能应对未来挑战的组织。

This is why we emphasize starting small and iterating. Instead of trying to transform everything at once, you’re planting seeds that will hopefully grow over time. The RFC process might evolve into a sophisticated architecture review system. Basic metrics might become the foundation of an engineering insights platform. That daily standup might transform into a highly coordinated delivery system. However, none of this happens overnight, and attempting to skip directly to the end state usually fails.

这就是为什么我们强调从小处起步、不断迭代。与其试图一次性改变一切，不如种下种子，希望它们随时间生长。RFC 流程可能演进成一套精密的架构评审体系。基础指标可能成为一个工程洞察平台的地基。那次每日站会可能蜕变成一个高度协同的交付系统。然而，这一切都不会一夜发生；试图直接跳到终局，通常会失败。

The evolution also applies to you as a leader. Every challenge you navigate, every crisis you resolve, and every team you build adds to your capability. You develop instincts about what works and what doesn’t. You learn to read the signs of impending problems. You build a network of relationships that can provide support and guidance. You create a reputation that gives you credibility and influence. These accumulated capabilities make you more effective over time, able to handle greater challenges with less stress.

这种演进也适用于作为领导者的你。你驾驭的每一个挑战、解决的每一场危机、搭建的每一支团队，都在为你的能力添砖加瓦。你会培养出关于“什么管用、什么不管用”的直觉。你学会读懂迫近问题的信号。你建立起一张能提供支持和指引的关系网。你积累出让你拥有信誉和影响力的声望。这些累积起来的能力，让你随时间变得更有效，能以更少的压力应对更大的挑战。

The Reality: It’s Harder Than It Looks

现实：它比看起来更难

We need to be honest about something: everything we’ve discussed in this book is more complicated to implement than it sounds. When we say “build psychological safety,” it sounds straightforward. But in reality, it requires hundreds of small actions, consistent behavior over months or years, and the ability to maintain that consistency even when you’re exhausted, frustrated, or dealing with your own challenges.

我们必须诚实地说一件事：本书讨论的一切，落地起来都比听起来复杂得多。当我们说“建立心理安全”时，听起来很直接。但在现实中，它需要成百上千个微小的行动、需要数月乃至数年里一致的行为，还需要在你精疲力竭、灰心丧气、或自身正被各种挑战缠身时，仍能维持这种一致性。

When we say “set clear direction,” it may seem simple, but in reality, you’re making decisions with incomplete information, and then communicating those decisions to people who may disagree, while maintaining conviction even when you’re not entirely sure yourself. It means being wrong sometimes (or a lot) and admitting it without losing credibility. It means changing course when necessary without appearing indecisive.

当我们说“设定清晰方向”时，可能显得简单；但在现实中，你是在信息不完整的情况下做决策，然后把这些决策沟通给可能并不认同的人，同时即便你自己也并非完全确定，还要维持信念。它意味着你有时会错（甚至经常错），并且在不失去信誉的前提下承认错误。它意味着在必要时改变航向，却又不显得优柔寡断。

When we say “implement lightweight processes,” it might sound easy. However, it actually means constantly fighting against process inflation, pushing back against well-meaning additions that would slow things down, and maintaining discipline when everyone around you is adding complexity. It means being the one who says no to the process that would make one person’s work easier, because it would make everyone else’s work harder.

当我们说“落地轻量流程”时，可能听起来容易。然而它实际上意味着：持续对抗流程膨胀，抵制那些出于好意却会拖慢节奏的新增流程，并在周围所有人都在添乱时保持自律。它意味着：由你来说不——对那个会让某个人工作更轻松、却会让其他所有人工作更艰难的流程说不。

When we say “track meaningful metrics,” it might sound obvious. But, in reality, it means resisting the pressure to measure what’s easy rather than what matters, explaining again and again why certain metrics are misleading, and maintaining faith in your measurements even when they show things getting worse before they get better.

当我们说“追踪有意义的指标”时，可能听起来不言而喻。但在现实中，它意味着：抵制那种“去度量容易度量的东西而不是重要的东西”的压力，一遍又一遍地解释为什么某些指标会误导人，并在指标显示“情况在变好之前先变得更糟”时，仍然相信你的度量。

— 原书第 254 页 —

None of this is easy. All of it requires sustained effort, political capital, and emotional energy that you might not always have. There will be days when you want to give up, when things feel overwhelming, and when nothing you do seems to make a difference. These moments are not failures, and they are not unusual; they’re part of the journey. The difference between leaders who succeed in chaos and those who don’t isn’t that the successful ones don’t struggle; it’s that they keep going despite the struggle.

这一切都不容易。它们都需要持续的努力、政治资本和情绪能量——而这些你并非总是拥有。会有那么几天：你想放弃，一切让人喘不过气，你做什么似乎都无济于事。这些时刻不是失败，也并不罕见；它们是旅程的一部分。在混乱中成功的领导者与不成功的领导者之间，区别不在于成功者不挣扎；而在于他们尽管挣扎，仍然继续前行。

Those leaders also know that they need to manage that struggle, that stress, and those outcomes of expending all that emotional energy. You need to find outlets outside of work: friends, family, hobbies, and pets—whatever works for you. We both write articles and books in our spare time. (Though we don’t recommend this as an output.) Juan found solace in photography because film develops faster than organizations do. James continues to build productivity tools because code is honest in a way that management rarely is. And, as we’ve mentioned, sometimes those outlets are not enough. There’s no shame in walking away from something to protect your mental and physical health.

那些领导者也知道：他们需要管理那种挣扎、那种压力、以及耗尽所有情绪能量之后的那些结果。你需要在工作之外找到出口：朋友、家人、爱好、宠物——什么对你管用就用什么。我们俩都在业余时间写文章、写书。（不过我们不推荐把这当作一种宣泄出口。）Juan 在摄影中找到了慰藉，因为胶片显影比组织演进快得多。James 继续做效率工具，因为代码是诚实的——而管理工作很少如此。而且，正如我们提过的，有时候这些出口还不够。为了保护自己的身心健康而从某件事抽身，一点也不丢人。

The Practice: Making It Real

实践：让它成真

So, how do you implement all of this? How do you apply the concepts, frameworks, and principles that we’ve discussed to make them a reality in your specific situation? The answer is: gradually, intentionally, and with numerous adjustments along the way.

那么，你究竟该如何落地这一切？如何把我们讨论过的概念、框架和原则，应用到你具体的处境中、让它们成真？答案是：循序渐进、有意识地，并在途中做无数次调整。

Begin by taking stock of your current situation. Use the assessments and exercises that we’ve provided throughout the book. You don’t need to do them all at once, but pick the areas that feel most urgent or most achievable and start there. It may involve establishing basic technical principles, or maybe it’s implementing a simple RFC process. It could be as simple as starting daily standups that actually work. Whatever it is, pick one thing and commit to it for at least a month.

从盘点你的现状开始。使用我们在全书里提供的那些评估和练习。你不需要一次性全做，而是挑出那些感觉最紧迫、或最容易上手的领域，从那里开始。它可能涉及确立基本的技术原则，或者落地一个简单的 RFC 流程。它可能简单到只是开始开“真的管用”的每日站会。无论是什么，挑一件事，承诺至少做一个月。

As you implement that one thing, pay attention to how it lands with your team. Are they embracing it or resisting it? Is it solving the problem you thought it would, or creating new ones? Is it sustainable given your current constraints, or does it require constant energy to maintain? Use these observations to adjust your approach. Maybe the daily standup meeting needs to be asynchronous because of time zones, or maybe the RFC process needs to be even more lightweight. Perhaps the technical principles need to be more specific or more general.

在你落地这一件事的过程中，留意它在团队中的反响。他们是在拥抱它，还是在抵触它？它解决了你以为它会解决的问题，还是制造了新问题？在你当前的约束下它可持续吗，还是需要持续投入精力才能维持？用这些观察来调整你的方法。也许每日站会因为时区问题需要改成异步；也许 RFC 流程需要更轻量。也许技术原则需要更具体，或更概括。

Once that first focus area is working reasonably well, add something else. Don’t take on everything at once—just one more thing. Maybe now that you have daily standups working, you can add a lightweight planning session. Maybe now that you have basic technical principles, you can start code reviews that actually reference them. Maybe

当第一个聚焦领域运转得相当不错之后，再加一件事。不要一次承担一切——只加一件。也许既然每日站会已经跑顺了，你可以加一个轻量的计划会。也许既然你有了基本技术原则，你可以开始在代码评审里真正引用它们。也许

— 原书第 255 页 —

now that you have an RFC process, you can start tracking cycle time to see if it’s actually helping.

既然你有了 RFC 流程，你可以开始追踪周期时间，看看它是否真的有帮助。

This incremental approach might feel slow, especially when the chaos around you is screaming for immediate solutions to everything. But it’s the only approach that actually works in chaos. Trying to change everything at once just adds to the chaos. It overwhelms your team, dilutes your focus, and usually results in nothing really sticking. It’s better to make one real improvement that lasts than 10 superficial changes that evaporate under pressure.

这种渐进的做法可能让人觉得慢——尤其是当你周围的混乱在尖叫着要求立刻解决一切时。但它是混乱中唯一真正奏效的做法。试图一次性改变一切，只会给混乱添乱。它会压垮你的团队、稀释你的焦点，结果通常是什么都没真正留住。做出一个能持久的真实改进，胜过十个在压力下蒸发的表面变化。

Remember, too, that you don’t have to do this alone. Look for allies within your team and across the organization. Find the senior engineer who’s been holding things together (or hire one to do the holding) and make them your partner in change. Connect with the product manager who shares your vision for how things could work better. Build bridges with the operations team that’s dealing with the consequences of the current chaos. These relationships are force multipliers, relationships that enable you to drive change across multiple fronts simultaneously.

也请记住：你不必独自做这一切。在你的团队内部、在整个组织中寻找盟友。找到那个一直在撑着局面的高级工程师（或招一个来撑局面），让他成为你推动变革的伙伴。联系那位和你一样希望事情能变得更好的产品经理。和那个正在承受当前混乱后果的运维团队架起桥。这些关系是力量倍增器——它们让你能够同时在多条战线上推动变革。

The Future: Beyond Survival

未来：超越生存

Throughout this book, we’ve focused primarily on surviving and thriving in chaos. But what about after? What happens when the chaos subsides, when stability emerges, and you can finally catch your breath? The answer is that the capabilities you’ve built in chaos become superpowers in stability.

全书我们主要聚焦于在混乱中生存和茁壮成长。但之后呢？当混乱退去、当稳定出现、当你终于能喘一口气时，会发生什么？答案是：你在混乱中练就的能力，会在稳定中变成超能力。

Teams that have learned to make decisions with incomplete information become incredibly agile when they have good information. Engineers who have learned to ship imperfect solutions iteratively become masters at continuous delivery when they have the luxury of more time. Leaders who have learned to maintain psychological safety under extreme pressure create incredibly innovative cultures when the pressure eases.

那些学会在信息不完整时做决策的团队，在拥有充分信息时会变得极其敏捷。那些学会迭代式交付不完美方案的工程师，在拥有更多时间时会成为持续交付的大师。那些学会在极端压力下维持心理安全的领导者，在压力缓解后会创造出极具创新力的文化。

The technical principles that guided you through chaos become the foundation of a strong engineering culture. The lightweight processes that kept you moving become the seeds of more sophisticated systems. The metrics that helped you navigate uncertainty become the basis for continuous improvement. The relationships forged in crisis become the networks that drive future success.

那些带你穿越混乱的技术原则，会成为强大工程文化的地基。那些让你保持前进的轻量流程，会成为更精密系统的种子。那些帮你驾驭不确定性的指标，会成为持续改进的基础。那些在危机中结下的关系，会成为驱动未来成功的网络。

This is perhaps the most important message of this book: the work you do in chaos isn’t just about survival; it’s about building the future. Every improvement you make, every capability you build, and every relationship you strengthen is an investment that will pay dividends long after the current crisis has passed. You’re not just fighting fires; you’re building a fireproof foundation.

这也许是本书最重要的一条信息：你在混乱中做的工作，不只是为了生存；它是为了建造未来。你做出的每一次改进、你建立的每一项能力、你巩固的每一段关系，都是一笔投资——在当前危机过去很久之后，它仍会持续派息。你不只是在救火；你是在打一个防火的地基。

— 原书第 256 页 —

The Call: Your Turn to Lead

召唤：轮到你来领导了

So, here we are, at the end of our journey together through the chaos of engineering leadership. We’ve shared our experiences, our frameworks, our successes, and failures. We’ve tried to provide you with tools and techniques, principles and practices, as well as warnings and encouragement. But now, it’s your turn.

那么，我们走到了这里——走到了我们一同穿越工程领导力混乱之旅的终点。我们分享了自己的经历、框架、成功与失败。我们努力为你提供工具和技巧、原则和实践，以及警告和鼓励。但现在，轮到你了。

You’re the one in the arena, facing your specific chaos with your particular team in your unique context. No book can tell you exactly what to do in your situation. No framework can perfectly capture the complexity you’re dealing with. No principle can resolve every tension you face. Leadership in chaos is ultimately about judgment, courage, and persistence in the face of uncertainty.

你是那个站在竞技场里的人，在你独特的处境中，带着你那支特定的团队，面对你那份特定的混乱。没有哪本书能告诉你在你的处境里究竟该怎么做。没有哪个框架能完美捕捉你正在应对的复杂性。没有哪条原则能化解你面对的每一处张力。混乱中的领导力，归根结底是在不确定性面前的判断力、勇气和坚持。

But you’re not starting from zero. You have your experience, your instincts, and your relationships. You now have the knowledge that we’ve shared and the wisdom of others who have walked this path. You have a team that, despite everything, shows up every day and tries to build something meaningful. You can make things better, even if it’s just a little bit at a time.

但你不是从零开始。你有你的经验、你的直觉、你的关系。你现在拥有了我们分享的知识，以及那些走过这条路的人的智慧。你有一支团队——尽管历尽一切，仍然每天出现、努力建造一些有意义的东西。你能让事情变好，哪怕每次只变好一点点。

The chaos you’re facing isn’t a bug in the system; it’s increasingly the norm for the system. The world is moving fast, technology is becoming more complex, and organizations are more interconnected than ever. The ability to lead effectively in chaos isn’t just a nice-to-have skill; it’s become essential for engineering leadership at all levels.

你面对的混乱不是系统里的一个 bug；它正日益成为系统的常态。世界在快速变化，技术变得越来越复杂，组织之间比以往任何时候都更加互联。在混乱中有效领导的能力，不再只是一项锦上添花的技能；它已经成为各级工程领导力的必备能力。

This means that the work you’re doing matters more than you might realize. You’re not just keeping your team productive or your systems running. You’re developing and demonstrating a critical capability that organizations desperately need. You’re showing that it’s possible to build great software and great teams even when everything is uncertain. You’re proving that engineering excellence doesn’t require perfect conditions.

这意味着你正在做的工作，比你以为的更重要。你不只是在让团队保持产能、让系统保持运转。你正在培养并展示一种组织极度需要的关键能力。你在证明：即便一切都不确定，也有可能做出伟大的软件、打造伟大的团队。你在证明：工程卓越并不需要完美的条件。

Remember that leadership in chaos is not about being perfect but about being present. It’s about showing up consistently, even when you don’t have all the answers. It’s about making decisions when waiting isn’t an option. It’s about protecting your team while pushing them to grow, maintaining hope when things look bleak, and upholding humility when things go well.

请记住：混乱中的领导力不在于完美，而在于在场。它在于即便你没有所有答案，也始终如一地出现。它在于当等待不再是一个选项时，做出决策。它在于保护你的团队、同时推动他们成长；在于形势黯淡时保持希望；在于一切顺利时保持谦逊。

Remember, too, that you don’t have to be a hero. Despite our occasional metaphors about storms, engineering leadership isn’t about grand gestures or dramatic interventions. It’s about the accumulation of small, positive actions over time and the conversations that prevent a misunderstanding. Leadership is strongest in the processes that eliminate a recurring problem, in the decisions that unblock a team, and in the feedback that helps someone grow. These small acts, repeated consistently, create the conditions for success.

也请记住：你不必做英雄。尽管我们偶尔会用风暴打比方，工程领导力不在于宏大的姿态或戏剧性的干预。它在于随时间积累的微小而积极的行动，以及那些避免了一场误解的对话。领导力最坚实的体现，在于那个消除了反复出现问题的流程、那个解除了团队阻塞的决策、以及那段帮助某人成长的反馈。这些微小的行动，被一致地重复，创造出成功的条件。

— 原书第 257 页 —

Take care of yourself along the way. Leadership in chaos is exhausting, and burnout is very real. The same psychological safety you create for your team needs to extend to yourself. The same permission to fail that you give others needs to apply to your own efforts, and the same focus on sustainable pace that you preach needs to govern your own work. You can’t pour from an empty cup, and your team needs you to be able to sustain this effort over the long haul.

一路上，照顾好你自己。混乱中的领导令人精疲力竭，倦怠是非常真实的。你为团队创造的那种心理安全，也需要延伸到你自己身上。你给予他人的那种“允许失败”，也需要适用于你自己的努力。你所倡导的那种“可持续节奏”，也需要约束你自己的工作。空杯子倒不出水来，你的团队需要你能够长期地撑住这份努力。

Build your support network. Find other engineering leaders who understand what you’re going through. Join communities, attend meetups, and participate in online discussions. Share your experiences and learn from others. The specific solutions might not transfer, but the patterns do—and the emotional support certainly does. Knowing that others have faced similar challenges and survived can make all the difference on the hard days.

建立你的支持网络。找到那些懂你正在经历什么的其他工程领导者。加入社区、参加线下聚会、参与线上讨论。分享你的经历，向他人学习。具体的解决方案也许不能照搬，但模式可以——情绪支持更是如此。知道其他人也曾面对类似的挑战、并且活了下来，在那些艰难的日子里会带来天壤之别。

Keep learning, but be selective about it. There’s an endless stream of blog posts, books, podcasts, and conference talks about engineering leadership. Not all of it will be relevant to your situation and not all of it will be good advice. Learn to filter for what’s useful, what’s applicable, and what’s worth your limited time and energy. Sometimes the best learning comes not from consuming more content but from reflecting on your own experiences.

持续学习，但要有选择。关于工程领导力的博客、书、播客和大会演讲无穷无尽。并非所有内容都与你的处境相关，也并非所有内容都是好建议。学会筛选：什么有用、什么适用、什么值得你有限的时间和精力。有时候最好的学习，不是来自消费更多内容，而是来自反思你自己的经历。

Finally, maintain perspective. The chaos you’re dealing with today will eventually pass (and, in fairness, it might pass because your organization doesn’t survive). The crisis that seems overwhelming now will become a story that you tell future teams. The impossible challenge will become a capability that you’ve built. This doesn’t minimize the difficulty of what you’re facing, but it reminds you that it’s temporary. You will get through this, your team will get through this, and you’ll all be stronger for it.

最后，保持视角。你今天正在应对的混乱终将过去（公平地说，它也可能因为你的组织没能撑过去而过去）。如今看似压得人喘不过气的危机，会变成你讲给未来团队听的故事。那个不可能的挑战，会变成你练就的一项能力。这不是在淡化你所面对的困难，而是在提醒你：它是暂时的。你会度过这一切，你的团队会度过这一切，而你们都会因此变得更强。

The End, and the Beginning

终章，亦是序章

As we close this book, we want to leave you with one final thought: engineering leadership in chaos is not a problem to be solved but a practice to be developed. You don’t “fix” chaos and then move on. You develop the skills to navigate uncertainty, the judgment to make decisions with incomplete information, and the resilience to keep going when things get tough.

在合上书之际，我们想留给你最后一句话：混乱中的工程领导力，不是一个待解决的问题，而是一种待修炼的实践。你不是把混乱“修好了”然后转身离开。你培养的是驾驭不确定性的技能、在信息不完整时做决策的判断力、以及在艰难时刻坚持下去的韧性。

You’ve chosen a difficult path. Engineering leadership is challenging enough in stable conditions. In chaos, it can feel impossible. However, it’s also incredibly rewarding. There’s something pretty cool about taking a group of individuals and helping them become more than the sum of their parts. It’s meaningful to create order from disorder and build something valuable despite overwhelming odds. Sometimes you can prove that chaos doesn’t have to mean dysfunction, that uncertainty doesn’t have to mean paralysis, and that difficulty doesn’t have to mean failure.

你选了一条艰难的路。工程领导力在稳定条件下已经够有挑战了。在混乱中，它可能让人觉得根本不可能。然而，它也带来无比丰厚的回报。把一群独立的个人，帮助他们变成大于各部分之和的整体——这是一件相当酷的事。从失序中创造秩序、在压倒性的劣势下建造出有价值的东西——这是有意义的。有时候你可以证明：混乱不必意味着功能失调，不确定不必意味着瘫痪，艰难不必意味着失败。

— 原书第 258 页 —

Your team needs you—not to have all the answers, but to help them find answers; not to eliminate all uncertainty, but to help them navigate it; not to protect them from all challenges, but to help them grow through challenges. They need you to be the leader we’ve described throughout this book: present, consistent, thoughtful, and human.

你的团队需要你——不是需要你拥有所有答案，而是需要你帮他们找到答案；不是需要你消除所有不确定性，而是需要你帮他们驾驭它；不是需要你保护他们免于一切挑战，而是需要你帮他们在挑战中成长。他们需要你成为我们在全书里描述的那种领导者：在场、一致、体贴、且有人情味。

Your organization needs you, too, whether they fully realize it or not. Who can deliver results despite imperfect conditions? Who can build great teams without unlimited resources? Who can make progress without perfect information? Who can maintain technical excellence while navigating business reality? Well, we think it’s you. The skills you’re developing and the capabilities you’re building are exactly what most organizations need.

你的组织也需要你——无论他们是否完全意识到。谁能在不完美的条件下交付结果？谁能在资源有限的情况下打造伟大的团队？谁能在信息不完美时取得进展？谁能在应对商业现实的同时维持技术卓越？我们认为，那个人就是你。你正在培养的技能、你正在建立的能力，正是大多数组织所需要的。

So, go forth and lead! Take what we’ve shared and make it your own. Adapt it to your context, evolve it based on your experience, and share what you learn with others. Build great software, but more importantly, build great teams. Create technical excellence, but also create human connections. Drive results, but also drive growth, human and otherwise.

那么，去吧，去领导！把我们分享的东西变成你自己的。把它适配到你的处境里，基于你的经验去演进，并把你学到的分享给他人。构建伟大的软件，但更重要的是，构建伟大的团队。创造技术卓越，但也创造人际连接。驱动结果，但也驱动成长——无论人的成长还是其他方面的成长。

This is your time. This is your challenge. This is your opportunity to make a real difference in your team, your organization, and your own career. The path won’t be easy, but it can be worthwhile. And remember, you’re not alone: lean on your support network for advice (and comfort) or as a place to vent.

这是你的时代。这是你的挑战。这是你的机会——去为你的团队、你的组织、以及你自己的职业生涯带来真正的改变。这条路不会轻松，但它值得走。而且请记住，你并不孤单：倚靠你的支持网络，向它寻求建议（和安慰），或把它当作一个宣泄的出口。

Welcome to engineering leadership in chaos. It’s messy, it’s difficult, and it’s often (or occasionally) thankless. However, it’s also where the real work happens, where important problems get solved, and where the future is built. One small improvement at a time, one decision at a time, and one day at a time, you’re making things better. And that’s what leadership really means.

欢迎来到混乱中的工程领导力。它一团糟、它很艰难，而且常常（或偶尔）吃力不讨好。然而，也正是在这里，真正的工作得以发生，重要的问题得以解决，未来得以被建造。一次一个小改进，一次一个决策，一天一天地过，你正在让事情变得更好。而这，才是领导力真正的含义。

Keep going. Keep learning. Keep leading. The chaos needs you, and more importantly, your team needs you. You’ve got this, even when it doesn’t feel like it. Especially when it doesn’t feel like it—that’s when real leadership happens.

继续前行。持续学习。持续领导。混乱需要你，更重要的是，你的团队需要你。你能行——即便感觉不像能行的时候。尤其是在感觉不像能行的时候——那才是真正的领导力发生的时刻。

Now put down this book, take a breath, and make something better than it was yesterday. That’s the work. Chaos isn’t going anywhere. But neither are you. And that’s what matters.

现在，放下这本书，吸一口气，去把某件事做得比昨天更好。这就是那份工作。混乱不会自己走开。但你也不会走开。而这，才是最重要的。
